newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Reform key for secure Russian investment-professor.
newsitem.headline: Reform key for secure Russian investment-professor.

text.p: Reformers at the top of Russian government must succeed in beating corruption if the country is to offer security for investors, delegates at the Financial Times Gold Conference heard on Tuesday.

Professor Peter Frank from Britain's University of Essex said the stability and orderliness of Russia would determine whether or not similar conditions could be created throughout the former Soviet Union.

Whether or not attempts to clean up crime and introduce order would succeed depended in the short term on President Boris Yeltsin remaining healthy enough to stay in office and on Yeltsin continuing to support reform, he said.
The investment risk is less than it was a year ago, Frank said, but few of Russia's critical problems have been solved.
With the collapse of Communism Russia acquired "a super-abundance of freedom" but it also lost the institutions which had given shape to the Soviet state.
Frank said there were three fundamental principles which a democracy must fulfil - choice, accountability and the rule of law.
Russia has established choice through elections and moved towards a mixed economy but government accountability remained weak and the rule of law was almost non existent.
"Of the three, the rule of law must be the most fundamental," Frank said.
He said Russia was an "institutionally under-developed state" and this immaturity would impact anybody wanting to do business with it.
International financier George Soros described what was being created in Russia as "robber capitalism" and Yeltsin also recognised the problem, Frank said.
In his 1994 state-of-the-nation address, Yeltsin looked forward to stabilisation of the investment process and said that crime was a threat to Russia's national security.
Now the reformist endeavours of the cabinet team headed by Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov have made a bold start but they would make many enemies and success was not yet certain, Frank aid.
"The institutionalisation of democracy still has a long way to go," he said.
